[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The closest measured context, cerivastatin, shares the 3,5-dihydroxyhept-6-enoic acid side chain and a fluorophenyl substituent and had absolute oral bioavailability 60% (90% CI 51-70%) in fasted healthy young men, with the lower bound well above the 20% threshold.

L3 card C83 shows that after an oral pitavastatin microdose, the pitavastatin lactone metabolite was measurable in plasma (rifampin GMR ~0.9 for Cmax and AUC), confirming oral absorption and systemic exposure of the pitavastatin scaffold; this is supportive but does not quantify absolute F.

L4 cards C147, C130, C154, C128, and C114 support adequate solubility/dissolution and intestinal permeability for the acidic statin class (cerivastatin sodium freely soluble with rapid dissolution; atorvastatin Caco-2 AP-BL Papp 1.8e-6 cm/s; pH-dependent solubility for acidic statins).

L5 card C193 shows cerivastatin undergoes intestinal CYP3A metabolism, yet the same molecule has measured F=60% (C10/C18), so intestinal metabolism in this class does not imply F<20%; L5 cards C198/C179 show fluvastatin is an OATP2B1 substrate, supporting possible intestinal uptake for the statin side-chain class, while no pitavastatin-specific efflux/metabolism record is present.

L6 cards C249 and C215 provide pitavastatin-specific metabolic-stability evidence: pitavastatin lactone had low intrinsic clearance in human hepatic microsomes (4.6 µl/min/mg protein), and no marked difference in intrinsic clearance was detected between pitavastatin and its lactone form, supporting low hepatic first-pass metabolism for the free acid.

L6 records for fluvastatin (C224/C210/C212) and cerivastatin (C222/C241) show higher HLM intrinsic clearance, but these are different statin cores and do not transfer as low-F evidence to pitavastatin.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for pitavastatin free acid is present in the supplied cards.
No pitavastatin-specific hepatic uptake/biliary excretion or transporter record is present; low HLM intrinsic clearance does not by itself exclude transporter-mediated hepatic first-pass extraction.
Transfer from cerivastatin F=60% does not control for differences in the quinoline/cyclopropyl core versus the cerivastatin pyridine core, transporter profile, or first-pass metabolism.
The pitavastatin-specific L6 clearance record is for the lactone form; C215 bridges to the free acid but is not a direct free-acid clearance measurement.
No direct pitavastatin-specific intestinal permeability or efflux measurement is present; L4/L5 rely on class analogs.
content.decision_summary: Query is pitavastatin free acid. The closest measured context, cerivastatin, has absolute oral bioavailability 60% (90% CI 51-70%), far above the 20% threshold. L3 confirms oral absorption of the pitavastatin scaffold; L4 supports statin-class solubility and permeability; L5 adds only mechanistic gut-wall efflux/intestinal-metabolism evidence for other statins, with the closest cerivastatin card showing intestinal CYP3A metabolism yet F=60%. L6 adds pitavastatin-specific metabolic-stability evidence (low HLM intrinsic clearance for pitavastatin lactone, no marked difference vs free acid), supporting low hepatic first-pass metabolism. No transferable threshold-relevant low-F evidence appears. Prediction remains high, with strengthened confidence.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
